utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All the accused are here. Representation is exactly as it was yesterday; that means only Mr. Nikolic for the Beara Defence team missing. Okay. Good morning to you, General, and welcome back. We are going to proceed with your testimony. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, you were talking about the absence and standing in for a commander. What is the situation with the Chief of Staff? Who replaces the Chief of Staff when he's absent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the absence of the Chief of Staff, the most senior officer stands in for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you another training book. That's not the one we talked about yesterday. This is Exhibit 5P -- P3178. This is an exhibit from the Prosecutor's case. Actually, the relevance of this training book is that it is more legible than the one we were looking at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need, please, the following page. Could we please zoom in and enlarge on the bottom part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So yesterday, we talked about the function of the Chief of Staff who at the same time is the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move to the following page, please, and I need to show the first part of this page. Now, what you can see on this page is the Administration in Charge of Operational Affairs and Training, and one sees that next to the function of the chief of this administration, there is no mention that this is the Deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, what is the influence of this fact on the powers and the competences and the authorities of the Chief of Administration in Charge of Operational Affairs and Training when the Chief of Staff is absent?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I'm not sure whether we understood each other properly. I heard from the translator that this is a training book. Actually, what I'm seeing here is a working map of the personnel organs. Based on the extracts from the establishment papers - this is the first three column - they fill in the data relating to the actual situation in the VRS. And based on this map, they follow whether any positions are filled or not. In this particular instance, in the operations and training administration, the establishment position has been filled properly, and you can see that after Major General Dragutin Ilic came, Miletic -- Radivoje Colonel, Miletic Radivoj. This is consistent with what the information show. The chief of the administration and training -- training and operation administration is at equal footing with other chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, when you say that the chief of the administration for operational affairs and training is at the same level as the other chiefs, can you please explain what other chiefs you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I was referring to the chiefs of branches.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, this training book, according to this booklet, can you conclude who in the staff of the Main Staff would have replaced General Milovanovic in his absence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might conclude that under normal circumstances, the first one to stand in would be General Miletic, but one also can conclude that if the Chief of Staff goes away, he appoints someone else to stand in for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When the Chief of Staff is temporarily absent, what were the functions of the person who would stand for him -- stand in for him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person standing in at the time are consistent with the period of absence, which means that on his behalf he can only do the things that are urgent at that moment and nothing beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When a person stands in for the Chief of Staff who is temporarily absent and if in the period of that replacement the commander is also absent, does the person who replaces the Chief of Staff also automatically assume the functions of deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the function of the deputy commander does not exist per se, he cannot discharge these duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in that case when there is no Chief of Staff and no commander, the person who stands in for the Chief of Staff, does that person also replace the commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no way for this person to replace the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please explain the difference between "standing in for" and "replacing" somebody?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The difference is very clear. Replacement is a temporary action for a certain duration in a certain place and is implemented only in emergency situations. Rather, decisions can be made and they are very limited in nature. Certain things should be just noted, some basic things should be resolved, and if there is an emergency in combat operations he is devoid of any right of taking decisions. Standing in is a status in the service when all the jurisdiction areas are transferred to another person. The difference between the person standing in and the one who actually discharged his duties is virtually non-existent, and the only thing that should be underlined is that it is limited in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D753. This is the Law Pertaining to the Army from the 1st of June 1992, the law from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what I need is page 15 in B/C/S and 59 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think that there is a mistake in the interpretation -- in translation in English. I'd like to read -- I'd like to ask you to read out loud Article 156.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "An officer who is temporarily unable to carry out his duties will be assigned and stand in on a temporary basis per establishment. A standing person can carry out other duties in addition to his regular duties, and this assignment cannot last longer than six months or up to one year if so decided by a second superior officer."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please explain -- I think yesterday you touched upon it. Could you please, though, explain what according to the law the expression "temporarily prevented" means?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be temporarily prevented means that the officer assigned to a post is unable to carry out his duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, what about this senior officer? Is that person prevented from exercising his duties when he's in the area of his unit but not at the post of command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. No officer, especially of that rank, can and discharge duties from that post. His work-place is the entire zone. The Chief of Staff, his work-place, is actually the whole of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not know about the others, but I have a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, it's working now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in our case General Milovanovic, head of staff, was in at the period of time at the post of advanced command. In that particular case, in such a case, if -- was General Milovanovic prevented from assuming or exercising his functions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't have a problem with the question as a general proposition, but it calls for a factual conclusion. "Whether he's within the zone of responsibility and prevented otherwise from exercising his functions?" is a factual question, which this witness is not qualified to answer. If it's by virtue of his absent solely, then I think he is, but if it relates to certain circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- concerning the absence, that's a difference question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see your point. I can see your point. I think -- yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Ms. Fauveau, please. Thank you, both, for your pragmatism.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in the Army of Republika Srpska, the Chief of Staff -- can the Chief of Staff exercise his functions of advanced command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an indirect answer. First of all, the notion of a forward command post involves several command posts: the basic one, the forward one, and the rear one, not to mention the reserve or any other. Altogether, they constitute a command post, which means in whichever of these posts he is, he is at the command post and, therefore, exercising his duties relevant for that post.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, I think you said -- we have a problem in the transcript on page 6, line 18 and 19. You talked -- you were talking about several posts in the command structure. The position which is the basic one, the post that is the forward one, and the logistics position, what about all of these positions? What do they boil down to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might sometime over-do my precision talking. There is a single command post which is composed of several elements. One of the elements of a command post is the basic command post. Another element is the forward command post; therefore, a command post is a system made of a number of other systems and sub-systems. So wherever you are, either in one of the systems or sub-systems, you are within the system itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What are the consequences of representation? How is representation reflected on the status of the officer who stands in for someone or replaces or represents that person?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequences of representations are if a person is represented by someone and the position is vacant, the person who had been in this position previously cannot continue to do the duties, and the one assigned as the representative will discharge full duties and, therefore, enjoy all the rights and responsibilities to carry out his duties in the best possible way; and of course, in compliance with his performance he would be incentuised [as interpreted] to do his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, does representation have a consequence on the officer who stands in for somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "reward" or "incentive," I meant pay, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of Article 156 of the Law of the Army that you have before you, there is one decision that is mentioned. Could you please say what decision is referred to in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of this article, two things are mentioned; that is to say, that the replacement can't last no longer than six months, upon a decision of one officer and another officer, and that both replacements have to be based on a decision. Actually, an order is issued to that effect, and it contains specific elements as to which post is to be replaced, who is going to be the replacement, in what capacity, and what the duration would be, but it cannot extend the period of six months.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, is it possible to be a representative according to the law with all of the legal consequences without there being a written decision about it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not possible. A huge array of regulations govern this; one is the law, the regulations on financial activities, the rules of service, and without any of these rules, no valid decision can be taken. And in that situation, no subordinate is -- can be forced to carry out the order issued under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What about the decisions about representation? Could they be found in the personal dossier of an officer? I mean, if you look if the personal file of an officer, can you find a decision about representation if there was such a decision?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a crucial decision for the status and service of every officer, and it must be found. There is no talking about whether it can or cannot be found because many other consequences stem from that decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if from a linguistic standpoint, both in the JNA, as in the Army of Republika Srpska, the difference between replacement and representation was always made?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's an essential and professional difference, and every soldier has this difference, distinction in his blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would now like to show you Exhibit P412. I'd like to show you two rules now. The first one is P412. This is a rule pertaining to the corps of the army, the land army of the JNA. And I would like to have page 36 in B/C/S and 22 in English, please. In the paragraph just before 58, you can read that the chief of the operational application is the Chief of Staff, the Deputy Chief of Staff, and the B/C/S takes -- uses the word "replacement" or "replaces." Can you see this text?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to be shown P410. P410 is The Rules Concerning the Responsibilities of the Corps of the Land Army, Land Forces, in Peacetime. This also is rules from the former JNA. Could you give us page 12 in B/C/S and 10 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you read the paragraph number 2, sub-paragraph of number 13, because there is a mistake in the English translation of this sentence. Can you read this sentence aloud, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Article 12 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, just before this Article 12, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the absence of the Chief of Staff, the chief of operations and training shall stand in for him."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this specific case, does the word "represent" have the same meaning as what is meant by "represents" according to the law?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That word has the same meaning, but two distinctions are important here. First, you showed me the rule of the ground forces, and then you showed me the rule on jurisdictions and competences of the ground forces rule. These are very different documents. The rule of the ground forces is intended for commands in order to creatively apply the provisions of that rule depending on the situation of their units, the situation on the ground, et cetera. It's not binding in any way. It is a guide-line, and we can understand very clearly that the rule of ground forces contains a recommendation that in the absence of this and that, he shall be replaced by so-and-so or so-and-so shall stand on him, which can or may not happen. Whereas, in this document, it is said very precisely, in the absence of the Chief of Staff, the chief of operations and training shall stand in for him, which means that this rule stipulates that in the absence of the Chief of Staff, an order may be issued to the effect that only the chief of operations and training may stand in for him, no one else. But, it has to happen pursuant to an order. It doesn't happen automatically. An order has to be issued to stipulate this stand-in.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: These two rules which I've shown you are for the corps. Could they also be applied automatically to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the fact that they differ in essence, one is a rule and the other is a rule book -- I don't know if this distinction can be translated properly. This --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, did you hear the interpreters? They would like the witness to repeat. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer concerning precisely my question, which was, Do these rules or can these rules be automatically applied to the Main Staff since they are rules which concern the corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither the rule of the ground forces nor the rule on competences of the ground forces corps may be applied to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now go back to your report, 5D759, Exhibit 759 of your report. In B/C/S, it will be page 19, and in English, page 25. What I am interested in is the last part -- sorry, a bit lower, the bottom of the page. It's the last paragraph, last paragraph within paragraph 51. It's the top of page 25 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you wrote that the fact that General Miletic signed a great number of documents as representative does not reflect the fact that he had the function of a representative. Could you explain your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the transcript, receiving the term "representative" repeatedly instead of "stand in," and I just want to make sure, A, that we're talking about the same thing since it's a relatively important concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the second thing is that in the report itself, the English translation uses the term "stand in."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That, I was thinking about myself, this last part of that. Yes, Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am concerned, I accept "standing in for" in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And incidentally, following the proceedings both yesterday and particularly today, this is how it has been translated almost all along, into English, in other words, because that was also something that I wanted to draw your attention to since you are probably following in French. Yes, not always. This is why most of the time, not always. So I suggest that if you are interested in this that you also try and follow on your monitor because most of the time it has been "standing in for," but sometimes it hasn't. And also, the way it's been translated in the document here has not always been... But anyway, I am saying this, of course, each time there is a variation it will not be taken by the Trial Chamber as prejudicial to the position taken by you or by the Prosecution or by anyone else, for that matter. It's still open for your presentations in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, but it's as I tell you. In this context, I accept "standing in for" as the proper expression. I would like to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How did you reach this conclusion and the fact that General Miletic signed a certain number of documents as representative or standing in for the Chief of Staff? Standing in for did not reflect the function of standing in.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, by studying a large number of documents that had been made available to me, all sorts of documents and enactments, and the distinction is important; second, from talking with competent officers with whom I had occasion to meet, officers of the VRS, I came to the conclusion and established the fact that he signed certain documents such as reports, information papers, et cetera, and not combat documents. In the following part of the report, I explained what combat documents mean. We can see that by not a single one of these signatures did he assume the role of Chief of Staff upon himself; rather, he was performing a service role. He signed these documents and he chose, I believe, an unfortunate form of signature, but it was nevertheless appropriate relative to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were the competences and the powers of General Miletic when he signed those documents as standing in for the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago, I did not quite understand the discussion between you and the other counsel, but it doesn't matter. I proceed from the factual situation. General Miletic never stood in the for the Chief of Staff, and he signed documents you could say strictly in keeping with the rule of service. But he did choose an unfortunate form of signature block. For a while he signed papers correctly, which means that when the Chief of Staff was not present at the basic command post and a report needed to be signed so that it could go forward from the basic command post, because this report needed to be sent urgently rather than via the forward command post, he signed for the Chief of Staff. That was correct and appropriate to the moment, to the document itself, and to the consequences arising from that. Later, when I read that General Milovanovic made it clear that did not like to be signed -- did not like anyone to sign on his behalf, another way of signature was chosen. General Miletic signed as a stand-in, but again, this form was chosen depending on the moment and appropriate to the document signed. This way of stand-in was chosen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness now be shown 5D1017, 1017, documents from the Drina Corps of the 4th of July, 1995. What I am interested in is paragraph 2 of this document where you can read: [In English] "Exceptionally, a unit commander may issue an order authorising a number of officers of the command, either individually or by function, and specify which documents they may sign and for a stamp to be affixed to their signature." [Interpretation] Here, we're talking of a document of the Drina Corps which applies obviously to the unit corps, Drina Corps as such, but I would like to know whether this sort of rule about the signature is usual in the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This paragraph 2 of this explanation developed in the Drina Corps can practically be viewed as taken over from the rule book on office procedures, and two things must be distinguished here: may be authorised to signed, but not may be authorised to issue a document. There was a tacit understanding that General Manojlo authorised General Miletic to sign operative reports and reports on combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I believe you have already answered, but to be quite sure and clear, does the authorisation to sign a document entail in itself the powers of an officer who normally should have signed the document in question?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, no. If you are authorised to sign something, then you are only authorised to something. If you are authorised to issue a document, then you would be able to both issue a document and sign it. This way an authorisation is given only to sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I consult my client just a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the basis of the document which you may have seen and analysed, could you tell us whether General Miletic in 1995 at any time, even when he was colonel, had the power belonging to the Chief of Staff? Did he have these powers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for a moment. In all the time he performed the duties of the chief of operations and training, he never had authorisations to perform the role of the Chief of Staff. Not a single one of the Chief of Staff's powers were transferred or assigned to General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When General Milovanovic was absent - and I am speaking of a very temporary absence - to whom were transmitted his functions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every moment, General Milovanovic kept all the competences of the Chief of Staff wherever he was on the territory of the Republika Srpska. He could not assign to anyone else any of his powers or competences.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D1279. For the transcript, this is a conversation of the Croatian collection, an intercept. Could the text be blown up a bit in B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this conversation, this intercept, at the very beginning of this conversation you can see that General Nicolai, Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR, wanted to speak to General Milovanovic or with someone who had the proper authority, and he eventually spoke to General Mladic. Was this usual in that it was indeed the superior officer who would take a conversation or a call who was for his subordinate in the absence of the subordinate officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an example of excellent functioning of the chain of command in the VRS. As far as I know, there were strict regulations governing contacts with the UNPROFOR in terms of who was allowed to maintain that contact and how. I see that one of the powers to maintain contact with the UNPROFOR was transferred from General Milovanovic -- was transferred from Mladic to Milovanovic. Since this power was transferred only to Milovanovic, only Mladic and Milovanovic had the competence and the authorisation, so only the two of them were authorised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to come back on what you say in your report, Exhibit 5D759, page 21 in B/C/S and page 26 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could paragraph 59 be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this paragraph, you indicate that the command of the Republika Srpska was defined at three levels: strategic, operational, and tactical. What is the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of the VRS, the strategic level is the Army of Republika Srpska or at least the main body of the forces of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were certain military actions commanded at the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategic operations are commanded solely from the strategic level, and in certain cases the strategic level command can also command operative --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... identifying or making the plans of the operations at the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command includes planning, as well, which means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt the answers, but the previous question and answer were not recorded in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and I wonder if he could complete those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's start with that first. I am taking you back, General, to a previous question that Madam Fauveau asked you. And the reason for doing so is that the transcript did not complete your -- did not register the complete answer that you gave. The questions was as follows: "Were certain military actions commanded at the strategic level?" And what we have in the transcript, which is incomplete, is as follows: "Strategic operations are commanded solely from the strategic level, and in certain cases the strategic level command can also command operative ..." Can you continue from there, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can also command operations or operational actions, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Turning to you, Madam Fauveau, I think you need to repeat your next question because it is also incomplete. And thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who planned the operations at the strategic level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that the strategic operations were commanded by the Main Staff of the VRS and if we know that an integral part of commanding is planning, then the answer is that the Main Staff of the VRS is in charge of planning the main operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the role of the Chief of Administration in Charge of Operational Affairs and Education for the planning of such actions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the process of planning these actions, this role doesn't alter at all. Operation and training organ monitors the status of the units and, based on the commander's decision, drafts documents required for carrying out a specific action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the role of the chief of administration in charge of operations for the execution of strategic operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His institution or, rather, his organisational unit, that is an operation centre where all the information are gathered -- is gathered, they collect the information and distribute it to officers, they update the states of individual units, and based on the decision of the commander they pass on these decisions forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. At line 19, we have a question which reflects the role of the chief of administration in charge of operations for the execution of strategic operations. In the previous answer, the witness refers to carrying out a specific action, and it's unclear whether or not the action he's referring to is a strategic operation, tactical operation, or just an operation. I wonder if we could just clarify that so at least the record is clear with respect to his role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if the General has understood what you said in the first place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not quite clear on the gentleman's comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Precisely. I asked you this question because I suspected that would have been your answer. Shall I take it to my hands, Madam Fauveau, or you do it? I think you need to refer him first to the previous answer so that he understands exactly what is the specific action more or less that it could have been referring to. I mean, you do it. You're perfectly capable of doing it. I will --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this part, when we were speaking of the planning and execution of operations, at what level of the operations or military actions do you refer -- did you refer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke about planning operations, we were talking about the operations commanded by the Main Staff of the VRS; in other words, strategic operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when you spoke -- I have to find the proper line. When you speak of the chief of the administration charged with operational affairs, we are indeed speaking of the chief of the administration who is in charge of operational and education of the Main Staff, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this clarify the questions of my colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it's a matter I can address on cross-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us which command in the Army of Republika Srpska was -- is at the operational level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several commanders at the operational levels. These are corps commanders, commander of the airforce and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Which are the tasks of the commands at the operational level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commands of operational forces command their units, which mean that they plan, organise, command, and control the operation of their units. They carry out operational actions to which other forces can be attached outside the corps itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What was the task of the Administration in Charge of Operational Affairs and Education in the planning of military actions at the operational level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military actions at the operational level ordered by the Main Staff of the VRS, once the plans had been prepared at a certain level and all the documents are in place, the order and the decision are sent over to the Main Staff of the VRS, and each person analyses their respective field of responsibility in order to see whether the planned action is consistent with the task. And if that is the case, then a proposal is made to the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS to approve this action. So his role is that within his jurisdiction he reviews the plan for the operation and either gives his approval or disapproval.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that these actions were prepared at a certain level. At what level were these actions prepared or the plans were prepared? At what level were they prepared?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the operational level. It is corps commands that prepare these decisions and orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us which command in the Army of the Republika Srpska was situated at the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They range practically from battalion to division, and the VRS had all these units. The highest tactical unit was a division.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: To clarify the transcript, in your answer -- in your preceding answer, one may read, at line 16, that the commander of the staff of the Republika Srpska approves the actions - and we are speaking about actions taken at the operational level - and after that, I think you were speaking of the chief of the Administration In Charge of Operations and Education. And according to the transcript, it seems that he was either giving or not giving his approval or he may have disapproved. So who approved those decisions? It is just to be absolutely sure. Who approved those decisions of the commander at the operational level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was exclusively approved by the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, and the assistant chief for operations and training does not issue any decisions. His only role, and within his purview, can give an opinion about the document that he received, for example, whether the decision and the order are in accordance with the decision of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We were speaking about the tactical level. Was the Administration in Charge of Operational and Educational Matters of the Main Staff, did it have a role to play in the preparation of operations at the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations are not carried out at the tactical level. It's combat operations, and in this particular case, this administration has no jurisdiction over the units engaged in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did it have a role to play in the planification of combat at the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has no jurisdiction on the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the Administration in Charge of Operational Matters have a role to play in the execution or performance? I am speaking of the administration at the level of the Main Staff, have a role to play in the execution of operations at the operational level which was prepared by the corps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All operations prepared by the corps based on the orders issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, through the operations centre or, rather, the Operations and Training Administration, which is part of it, received reports distributed to competent officers based on which a report was prepared for the competent command; or, based on these reports, the commander of the VRS can issue a corrective decision, which is then passed on further through the same channels.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I understand that this is the general position, but yesterday you said that there wasn't an operational centre for the Army of the Republika Srpska. Does this fact change the situation somewhat in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the reports are gathered in the same place, and that is at the communications centre. I said that a kind of makeshift solution was made for a communications centre to be functional.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did all the operations prepared by the corps at the operational level have the source or their basis in an order given by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid we might not understand each other. Various --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, one moment. The interpreters are having problems. If you could start your answer again, please, and go slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. All operations planned and organised by the Main Staff of the VRS were followed and monitored through back-feed information. All other activities and actions carried out other -- by other units from operational forces were not followed through because there were no direct orders for them to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How can one distinguish between an operation and other activity, a combat activity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last time that whether something is to be defined as an operation or not is up to the forces engaged in it, depending on the task, the objective to be achieved, and the level of command that had issued the decision. Therefore, for the activities, which are based on the decisions made by the Main Staff of the VRS and which involved the engagement of one or more operational and enforce unit, and for which it is -- says very precisely that their decisions should need approval, these are the operations that are run by the Main Staff of the VRS. All other combat activities are natural activities pursued by corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like to ask a few questions concerning the operational control and in your report 5D759, page 24 in B/C/S and page 29 in the English text. We have seen that there were three levels of command: strategical, operational, and tactical. Here, it's about operational control. Is this operational control linked to the operational level of the command, or is it universal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operational control mentioned on page 24 of my expert report, due to some previous or later misunderstandings, a definition was given here based and relied on the US forces and NATO. However, it cannot apply to the VRS. This form of operational control, as we see it here, in the Army of Yugoslavia or in the VRS or any other army that derived for the former Yugoslavia did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that in the Republika Srpska the strategic level was situated at the level of the Army of the Republika Srpska. Who took the decisions? Who made decisions at that level, at the strategical level?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what was the role of the supreme commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of the Commander-in-Chief or the Supreme Command is defined in the decision on establishing the Supreme Command, and his role derives from the first census, which means to ensure the coordination of all potentials of the VRS with a view to solving specific problems. That means that supreme commander, in such a manner, took over upon himself to -- by engaging all other resources of the state ensure coordination and successful solution for the problems by the VRS. This is how it was regulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 5D755. This is about a decision concerning the establishment of the Supreme Command, and, indeed, one may see here that the Supreme Command was established with an objective to coordinate and to improve the efficiency of the command system of the Republika Srpska's army. And in Article 2, one can see who are the members of the Supreme Command, and among these members there is no member of the Republika Srpska who was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is this usual, that no member of the army, and in particular the commander of the army, should not be a member of the Supreme Command; is it usual?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read Article 1 carefully, which says that "The Supreme Command of the Army of Republika Srpska is hereby established for the purpose of coordinating and improving the efficiency of the system of the Army of Republika Srpska," which means that conditions are being created for it to be more efficient and that the Supreme Command is made up of a large number of key figures, then one can say that Article 1 and Article 2 are in accordance and in harmony and that no one from the army is required to be there. Sometimes, this coordination, however, had to be pursued based on the situation in the army, and for that purpose in Article 3 it is stipulated that if and when necessary, members of the military can be included and involved in the work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you. How do you feel you're going time-wise?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, I think I'm within the 16 hours in question. I don't think I will go any further.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I don't think I will go beyond. Correction of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, we didn't resume after the break as we should have because there was a technical -- a major technical problem, which has only been resolved now. The understanding is that we will go right through until 1.45, a quarter to 2 without a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: We were talking about the Supreme Command before the break. Could the Supreme Command make decisions pertaining to military operations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, it could. It seems that sometimes it did exercise this power or possibility, although it shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the Supreme Command elaborate on its own without the Main Staff participating? Could it elaborate military documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer would be almost the same as to the previous question. By virtue of the very fact that the Supreme Command had the right to command the army, there was no law requiring the Supreme Command to involve the army in the development of military documents. Basically, in such cases the army should have been involved, always. You can see on the basis of some documents made by the Supreme Command that it developed certain documents without the involvement of a competent qualified military person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your report, Exhibit 5D759, on page 26 in the B/C/S version and 32 in the English version, and here referring to paragraph 71, you have indicated the various characteristics or features for command. The first principle is singleness of command, and the second one is subordination. Then you go on to explain what the singleness or uniqueness of command is. Can you please explain how this principle operated in light of the existence of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Organisationally speaking, they were set up rather well. The Supreme Command was supposed to pass on its decision to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and the commander of the VRS was supposed to forward -- to pass the decision on to units and commanders down the chain. So organisationally speaking, it functions in the best possible way. However, in my report in a later chapter, I explained that it can be skipped. But then again, there are mechanisms that recover the principle of singleness of command, but we will come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I would like now to show you Exhibit 5D1219, 1219. Now, this is a document from the president of the republic dated 9th of March, 1995, which is directly addressed to the Sarajevo Corps. How is it -- I mean, the fact that this document exists and that it is sent directly from the president of the republic to the corps, how is it that it has an influence on the respect of the principle of uniqueness of command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I am a military analyst and a military expert, I want to avoid getting into politics, but I will try to describe some very important features of this procedure. It's obvious that the president of the republic, the supreme commander, had received information that he knew originated from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that he was anxious to urgently get some details, and then for that purpose he sent a telegram to the corps commander without delay. If the corps commander had directly answered the president of the republic, the supreme commander, he would have broken the principle of single command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Can we show page 2 of this document. I would precisely like to show you the answer from the Sarajevo Corps. Now, what we have on the screen is the answer from the Sarajevo Corps to the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska. I would like to apologise, but I think that it's easier to speak as we have this answer before our eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have an English of translation of this?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document in English has only one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is the first page that we saw earlier? Okay. Let's proceed, and we can't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe we can have the translation in English on the ELMO, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the document exists, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please continue your answer, how come that the commander of the Sarajevo Corps answered or sent his reply to the Main Staff of the army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said based on the prior telegram sent by the supreme commander to the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, that if he had answered directly without putting in the know his direct superior, then the principle of single command in the VRS would have been breached; however, the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps acted in an extremely professional way. He sent this document to his direct superior, the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. He acquainted him with the situation and suggested a solution, and this is a perfect example of how the principle of single command is restored even though one step had been initially skipped.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 2 of this reply, we can see that this is a situation in which General Tolimir was in the Sarajevo Corps, and according from what we read this had an influence on the facts which were reported to the Main Staff and which were about the Sarajevo Corps. Can you please explain how the presence of deputy [as interpreted] commander of the Main Staff in a subordinated unit had an impact or an influence on the way the reports were presented?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt again, Your Honour. We have a reference to General Tolimir, I think, as a deputy commander of the Main Staff, and I think that's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. I talked about the assistant to the commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document -- first of all, General Tolimir acted as deputy co-commander in touring the corps. You can see that this inspection had been planned in advance and it was performed professionally. During this tour, this inspection tour, certain problems and deficiencies had been noted as pointed out by some of the officers of the corps. They believed since they had informed General Tolimir that General Tolimir would pass on that information to the commander of the VRS as would have been natural and that the commander of the VRS would inform the supreme commander. In this belief, they anticipated this sharing of information and created this document, which created a bit of a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at line 19 I think we have the same reference again. I don't know if that's what the witness is saying. If that's the case, it's fine. But I see it says: "General Tolimir acted as deputy commander in touring the corps..." And I just wonder if we could just clarify that or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- for the record at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam, if you could clarify it with the witness yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you explain tell us what the function of General Tolimir was in 1995, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir was assistant commander of the VRS for intelligence and security. He was never deputy commander nor could he have been deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in the system of command in the army of Republika Srpska, did the Ministry of Defence have a role?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the system of command. The Ministry of Defence was part of the government and had a totally different purpose and different objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness now be shown 5D1330, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, as you can see, this is a document that is sent by the Main Staff of the armed forces of Republika Srpska to the president of the republic. And in the first paragraph, you can see that the minister of defence has issued some orders relating to command and control in the army. Can you please tell us something about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen this document before. The thing is, the minister of defence issued an order regulating powers in settling or determining relationships within the service obstructing the function in the service. By analysing in detail the provisions of this order and the situation at the time in the VRS and by analysing in detail the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, it seems me that this order was inadequate. It stood in the way of redressing the situation in the service, and the reaction of the commander was, therefore, justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Earlier, we were talking of the principles for command, and in your report -- well, I don't think that it's really necessary for us to come back to that. You have indicated that the second principle is that of subordination. Was this principle of subordination respected in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did this system exist in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because successful command and successful performance of assignments and missions is based on that principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you now be shown 5D1363. Meanwhile, I just want to say that this is a document from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated the 2nd of June, 1995, which is sent to the command of the 28th Division and the Zepa Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: As we look at the first paragraph of this document, what can you say about the application of the principle of subordination in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion to look at a very extensive collection of documents of the BH Army, and I could note the following: They sought to observe the principle of subordination to the maximum possible, although in certain situations it was breached.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you have an explanation why in paragraph 2 the 28th Division and the Zepa Brigade were to directly refer to the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina for questions relating to the supply of weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain that, and this explanation must be put into context. If we know that it was the president Alija Izetbegovic who very often contacted the local authorities directly, and if we know that it was commanders of brigades who contacted them directly, we see that this was a direct connection without going through the superior command. The superior command of the 28th Division was the 2nd Corps, and for the 285th Brigade it was the 28th Division. And this was set up in that way in order to resolve the questions of replenishment and resupply even outside the limits of the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you Exhibit 5D1204. This is an order from the Main Staff dated 5th of September, 1993, and I'd like to show you page 4 of the B/C/S version, which is page 7 in the English version. Can we have the very bottom of the page in English because that's what I need, paragraph 11 at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this paragraph 11 and tell us why such an order was made necessary in 1993 and particularly the factor that the influence of parties, political parties, was forbidden?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, this is a very complex order. It deals with a large number of areas. The order emphasizes or points out a problem, suggests a way to resolve it, and it emphasizes also certain prohibitions. In this specific case, we see a very professional attitude, a very professional position that the army should remain outside the influence of political parties and depoliticised.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you define in the military terminology what a decision is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the most simplest terms, according to a military definition, a decision is a determination how to perform a certain assignment or a mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is the difference between a decision and an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order is an element of command, and command is the skill to implement these decisions. So this decision is a determination setting a goal, whereas an order is an element of command describing how to reach that goal.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now come back to your report, so Exhibit 5D759 on page 39 in B/C/S, 48 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in this paragraph, could you please show the bottom part, paragraph 107. In paragraph 107, you mention three methods by which the work is done: the full method, the abridged method, and the decision-making without consultations. First of all, can you please say what level of command applied or enforced the full method?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All methods of work relate to the tactical command and upwards, from the regiment and brigade up to the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the following page of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you to briefly write or describe the full method of working.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, we see the process of work of the command, and one of its characteristics is that it has many points of contact with other commands, so the procedure doesn't differ very much. The differences are more linguistic than anything else. Here, we see the complete method of work. We see it consists of 13 steps. It has to be followed strictly, and these 13 steps ensure that all the organs of the command from beginning to end are involved in decision-making. And each, according to its competences, propose the best possible solutions. This method of work is always applied when the time allows, and every command strives to ensure there is sufficient time to go through the entire process and to allow enough time to subordinate commands to also apply this method of work. This method of work is also applied in issuing documents of the highest order, such as orders to operative units. The abridged method is used when there is limited time, and you can see according to this schematic that the abridged method contains four steps less. Practically, all organs of the command are also involved in the process of decision-making, but the decision-making process itself is abbreviated. And the third method is the urgent method, when there is no time, and it's practically decision-making on the move when decisions are made very quickly and passed on very quickly to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit P699. This is the handbook for the work of command and staffs, and I would like to have page 60 in B/C/S. I'm sorry about this delay. I am looking for the number of page in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at number 2 -- or, rather, the two last paragraphs before sub-paragraph (b), before paragraph 104 and just before sub-paragraph (b). This is the paragraph that starts by "Team members..." and I would like to ask you to please read those two paragraphs because the English version has translated two words in B/C/S by the same word in English. So if you can read it now, maybe we can avoid this mistake.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Team members and other command organs with their assistant will formulate segments of the command relating to their respective area and shall submit them to the Assistant Chief of Staff for Operations. "The Assistant Chief of Staff for Operations shall formulate the final version of the organ" -- "of the order and will take care that it is technically processed and forwarded to the subordinate." I would just like to add that for technical reasons only, the term "training" has been omitted, but that happens often.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Apparently, we still have the translation of two words that have a different meaning in B/C/S. Well, first of all, I would like to ask you to tell us what is the difference between the formulation in the first paragraph, "to formulate," and "to put in form," which is what's in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a meeting, a civilian meeting, I provided an explanation that sealed to be helpful to them, and I am going to do it again. The Assistant Chief of Staff for Operations and Training provides a whole as if he were using Lego cubes, but he doesn't provide the content of the cubes. The Chief of Staff will provide the whole from these elements, whereas the elements themselves and the content will be decided by the competent officers from respective commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, concretely when one looks at these two paragraphs, what is the tasks of the members of the team and that of the other organs of the command structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of team members and other organs of the command is by abiding by the commander's proposals to prepare decisions from their respective areas, and once they have drafted these decisions, they should pass them on to the Assistant Chief of Staff for Operations and Training.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What, then, is the task of the person, the officer, in charge of operations and training?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once he receives all these elements, he puts them in the order as defined by this rule in order to arrive at a whole document, and then he hands over the document to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think you have already talked about this, but, you know, to be even more clear, can you please be very clear, what is the influence of the officer in charge of operational affairs and training on the content of a document, for instance, a directive or an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No influence. He has no influence on the content, but on the form the influence was strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And what do you have in mind when you talk about the form? Can you explain what it means in an order or in a directive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of a whole of a document implies that this directive or an order contains all the required elements, that they are put in the proper order and that these elements are in a sequence that will be efficient for the subordinate command. This sequence is prescribed, among other things, by this Manual for the Work of Commands and Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in this hand-book, in the paragraph you have read, this paragraph mentions the orders. What other military documents were also issued according to this process?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This procedure allows a whole array of procedures to be implemented. A directive can be drafted by applying this procedure by the Main Staff of the VRS, and on the basis of this directive the corps command can draft operational orders. And then based on the operational orders, brigade commands or regiment commands can -- which are tactical commands can draw up their own orders, and this is how we go down the whole chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 24 in B/C/S of this same exhibit, this same hand-book, page 22 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, and I think it's in paragraph 33 of this handbook, what are the elements which determine the choice of method of work to be used?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see here a detailed explanation of what I mentioned several times. The selection of a particular method of work is done at the -- based on the level of command, on the qualification of command, the structure and the quality of officers, and many other elements. However, one of the crucial parameters is the time-frame or the available time. The division of labour here is slightly more flexible in this document because this document is intended, also, for regiments, and regiments are on a much lower tactical level than the Main Staff; therefore, they require more details than the Main Staff of the VRS would require.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what the difference is between a directive and an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference between a directive and an order is primarily at the level where they are issued. There are two level of issuance for a directive, and I have provided a charter of that in my expertise. One level is the state level when you have a directive issued by the commander-in-chief, and the second level is strategic level when a strategic amount issues a directive. In terms of its content, a directive is not intended strictly to contain all the elements. It is something to give a steering or a direction, and it set up objectives to be achieved by the subordinate command. It is binding at the same time, but it is also a direction. An order, on the other hand, is an executive document which contains strictly defined decision, time, participants, and very often a decision can be divided into stages. In that manner, it narrows the space for the subordinate in terms of the institution; that is to say, it restricts his space for his imagination by putting him into a precise time-frame and space-frame.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Now, in your report you have analysed the Directive number 7, for the report -- this is Exhibit P5, but I don't need it right now. I would only like to ask you about this directive. On the basis of this directive and of documents which you have consulted, were you able to draw conclusions about the method which was used when those directives were elaborated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that a few numbers that were directives made it necessary for one to draw a highly likely conclusion. Therefore, my conclusion was that, for instance, a directive is never drafted by applying an abridged method because this is a long-term document without any time limits. It provides direction and steering, and I don't know and I don't believe that there is any directive done by either an abridged method or without consultations in history ever. Secondly, the source of this directive and the idea underlying it dates back to the analysis of combat readiness in 1994. The fact that the draft of this document was most probably completed on the 7th or 8th -- or 8th March, and the fact that was that it was most probably approved on the 16th and the 17th of March indicates that the only possible way that was applied in preparing this directive was the full method.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just before I move to the work on Directive number 7, I would like to show Exhibit 5D999.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Directive Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that you did not know the situation of the case in which a directive was put together on the abridged method of work, on the basis of that method. Now, the officer who worked on this directive told us here in court that this specific directive was devised on the basis of the abridged method. Can you say something about this, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this directive was prepared at the forward command post where at the time there were a sufficient number of officers for a valid decision to be taken required for such a directive. Whether all these officers were the first- or second-ranking people in their respective areas, I don't know, but I wouldn't agree that this was done by applying an abridged method or that it was done without consultation. One might conclude that at the forward command post there were enough competent officers from the command staff and some organs that they needed for taking this decision. Probably, what they didn't consider to be relevant, this directive seems to be shorter than the other ones. As far as I can remember, it is said that some of the elements will be taken over from the previous directive, and I see that as a proof that actually a full method of work was applied rather than the abridged method.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And about the officer in charge of operations who was not involved in the drawing up of this directive, but in theory, what is the role of the officer in charge of operational affairs and training in -- when an abridged method is used? Does he have a different role from his role if the full method is to be applied?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his task is always the same. His task is to prepare the directive pursuant to the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now come back to your report. This is Exhibit 5D759, on page 41 in B/C/S and 51 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In paragraph 109 -- well, you have already mentioned the analysis of the combat readiness of 1994. In this paragraph, you have indicated that the supreme commander ordered the preparation of the directive during the analysis of combat readiness. How did you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached this conclusion in two steps. The first step was when I analysed how the analysis of combat readiness was organised and implemented and what the corps commands had come up as suggestions and what measures were taken by the staff command and what were the decision of the state of the VRS, and the VRS one could have concluded that the idea for Directive 7 was based on this analysis of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now see 5D767 -- sorry, 967. This is the diary for the meeting about combat readiness for 1994 that was held on 29th and 30th of January, 1995. And I'd like to show page 2 in B/C/S and page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In this document, one sees that the president of the republic was to make a presentation at 1550 [as interpreted] a.m. about the political and military objectives for the future as well as the strategy about the conduct of the war and peace negotiations. Was this presentation to have a connection with directive -- the future Directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This is a classic form of reporting about the combat readiness. If you would look at all the former JNA armies, you would basically find everything identical. Only the names would be different. This is a classical approach that you have the commander-in-chief present there and that he is formulating the future policies of negotiations and prosecutions of war. And later on, we see the input of his associates and other people who were present at this briefing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we continue, one correction of the transcript. On page 17, line 4, this is 1750 p.m. Can we now move to page 4 in English, and in B/C/S we are still on page number 2, at the very bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At 2100, one sees that the main commander, the staff commander, were to talk about the position -- the tasks of the Army of Republika Srpska during the truce and the most important tasks in 1995. So there was to be a discussion about that. Now, was the future Directive number 7 to be somehow connected to this part of the briefing and of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The conclusions and tasks relating to the units of the VRS have most to do with it, but in this specific case I think that these tasks were assigned on the 5th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 3 in B/C/S. In English, we'll still be on page 4, at the bottom of page 4. So you can see that at 2200 there was a closing speech by the commander, and amongst other things he was to talk about the conclusions and short-term tasks and most important tasks for the Army of Republika Srpska in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What is normally the role or the objective for this part of the analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically, this is the final act of the analysis in which the commander of the VRS presents or, rather, accepts the evaluation of combat readiness according to all relevant elements; and on the basis of that, he imparts what he believes to be important and how he assesses combat readiness. This was preceded by the assessments by corps commanders that they should have provided them in time and on the basis of this and as well on the conclusions that very often are added on the spot during the meeting become part of this final act of the analysis of combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And right after that at 2230, one can see that proposals and conclusions and tasks for the Army of Republika Srpska in 1995 were to be formulated. And according to this document, one can see that the head of Administration in Charge of Operational Affairs and Training of the Main Staff as well as the chief of the organs in charge of operations and training of the units were entrusted with that formulation. Can you please tell us what the role of these organs were in the formulation of the proposals that are mentioned in this part?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
